newsitem.title: GERMANY: First day of German metals sector pay talks ends.
newsitem.headline: First day of German metals sector pay talks ends.

text.p: German engineering trade union IG Metall and metal industry employers broke off talks on Monday evening after the first day of what is expected to be a marathon session on the 1997 pay round.

Leaving the talks, IG Metall chairman Klaus Zwickel refused to comment on how the five-hour session with the heads of employers' association Gesamtmetall went, but said talks would resume Tuesday morning.

Zwickel said earlier he expected the negotiations, in which the companies aim to cut sick pay and other benefits, to be very difficult. "I wouldn't like to pre-judge what our chances are, but the room for manoeuvre is very narrow."
The talks are expected to continue until Wednesday.

IG Metall repeated threats that unless the two make progress towards an agreement on future labour costs in the sector, workers are set to launch a second day of nationwide protests across the sector on Thursday.
Gesamtmetall says non-wage labour costs are crippling German competitiveness and reducing them is an absolute priority.

Gestamtmetall president Werner Stumpfe, in an article in the newspaper Handelsblatt on Monday, argued that the loss of around a million jobs since 1991 in an industry which currently employs some 3.5 million, was largely the result of high laboutr costs.

But Stumpfe displayed a softer line on legislation this month which allows employers to reduce sick pay to 80 percent of salary instead of 100 percent. The new law on sick pay should be reflected in the wage deal about to be negotiated, he said.
Stumpfe's initial advice was that metal and engineering employers should impose the sick pay cut immediately.

Gesamtmetall was forced to retract that recommendation, after firms including Daimler-Benz AG which acted on the recommendation were hit by mass protests involving more than 100,000 workers around the country.
IG Metall is going into the talks demanding that employers declare once and for all their position on the sick pay issue.
It is also demanding concrete job protection measures as part of the 1997 wage agreement, and has set aside more than half of its 1997 wage demand for such measures.

That would pave the way for a headline increase in wages of barely higher than inflation -- a rise that Gesamtmetall has said it could discuss if accompanied by measures that would significantly cut non-wage costs.

Gesamtmetall has said that an IG Metall offer to accept sick payments based purely on a worker's basic pay -- instead of an amount including an average amount of overtime -- would not bring in a sufficient cost reduction.

It estimates that would only save around a quarter of the costs that a 20 percent sick payment reduction would. That in turn has been calculated as saving German industry some 12 billion marks a year.
